vadi: Ma shuddh (Madhyam — M) — the relationship between shuddh and teevra Ma is the defining feature

notes_used: Both Ma shuddh (M) and Ma teevra (M#) are used in the same raag — this dual Madhyam is the raag's single most defining characteristic. Pa is present but approached in a vakra (oblique/zigzag) manner, not directly.

therapy_note: Kedar is a profoundly devotional raag — specifically associated with worship of Shiva. The use of both Madhyams (shuddh and teevra) in the same raag is unusual and creates a shimmering, otherworldly quality, as though moving between the mundane and the sacred. The vakra (zigzag) movement around Pa gives it a circling, meditative character. Singing Kedar in the evening creates a sense of divine presence.

bollywood_references.title: Mera Saya Saath Hoga
bollywood_references.note: Sometimes cited as Kedar-influenced — treat with caution

notes_for_vocalist: The dual Madhyam is the heart of Kedar — Ma shuddh and Ma teevra both appear, and the movement between them creates the raag's identity. Pa IS present in Kedar but it is approached in a vakra (oblique/zigzag) manner, not directly in a straight scale ascent. Teevra Ma is NOT the sole vadi — rather, the relationship between the two Mas is what defines the raag. Do not reduce this to 'just use teevra Ma.'
common_mistakes: Treating Pa as absent — Pa is present in Kedar, approached vakra
Treating only teevra Ma as important and ignoring shuddh Ma — both are essential
Singing Pa in a straight ascending scale — it must be approached obliquely (vakra)
Confusing with Yaman, which also uses teevra Ma but has a completely different structure
variant_notes: Kedar's treatment varies significantly by gharana. Sa's role, the exact vakra movements, and how the two Madhyams interact all show variation. Some renditions use Sa quite minimally; others include it normally.
